doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the conch shell
title: Rahsaan as first grand master, and the lesson 'this is Duke Ellington'
summary: Turré describes Rahsaan's open approach, blindness and self-taught genius, and the night at the Both/And when Rahsaan told him not to play J.J. on Ellington.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: It is interesting that he could have been — just if he played tenor sax he would have been like a major contributor to the jazz lexicon I guess is what I’m trying to say but and of course in addition he had all that other things that he did.

You know what’s interesting? I mean to me Rahsaan is the first grand master that I’ve played with and then later on, once I came to New York I played with him again up until he passed. But he could play anything. I mean musically. Spiritual things man. And he was encouraging but at the same time he would tell you like it is and sometimes it would hurt, or sometimes it was like a slap, a wake-up. You know? Listen. All that counts. Because I remember he played the whole history of the music in the course of the night if the music went there. And he wasn’t imitating Sidney Bechet’s licks or whoever’s licks. He was being himself within the style of that music. You know, he was self taught. He didn’t go to school. If he had a gone to school they would have told him you can’t play three saxophones at once, it would have never happened. The stuff he was doing with flute man a flute teacher would have a fit. You know. So, but it’s beautiful music. And we would rehearse and get to the gigs and sometimes he wouldn’t even play what we rehearsed and he’d just start playing and we’d have to listen and go with it. And of course rehearsing with him wasn’t by a piece of paper because he is blind. You just have to listen and learn. All that stuff made a big difference in my conception and perception of the music. I remember one time, you know, I knew something about New Orleans music. And I knew something about bebop because I was into J.J. So Kid Ory and J.J. But I missed the stuff that came in between. And so one time we were playing at a club called the Both/And in San Francisco. And he played an Ellington tune I think. Maybe “Satin Doll,” I can’t remember, it was ‘68 or something, it was a long time ago. But he played then I played, the piano was taking a solo and he tells me, right on the stage, I mean he didn’t shout out it but he said, “Man, don’t be playing no J.J. Johnson, this is Duke Ellington.” And so I just said okay. And then afterwards we were in the dressing room and I asked him, I said, “What did you mean?” He said, “Well it’s a different phrase, it’s a different vernacular, it’s a different language. It’s connected through the blues, it’s still an extension of language, but the phrasing is a little different. You know, and he took me to his hotel room and he had one of them little portable record players and he used to carry two suitcases, one had records and a little player and the other one was clothes and stuff. And, oh you’d die, he had a duffel bag, like a big military duffel bag and he’d put his saxophones in.

It’s funny you mention that because I recall watching, that time I saw him, he sort of made me nervous with his horns. I’m a saxophone player too, so you know he was surrounded by his instruments and of course he was blind, so he’d be reaching all over.
And I felt like I wanted to go up and help him. Odd feeling. So he had his horns in a duffel bag, huh?
